sections.body: This field examines how AI changes the production, review, and trustworthiness of research. It is not mainly about abstract ethics, it is about concrete decisions: who is listed as an author, whether a citation exists, where training data came from, how an ethics board reviews a project, and whether an image or dataset can be traced to its source. AI is now used to draft manuscripts, suggest references, screen literature, assist ethics review, and generate or edit images. Those uses create new failure modes, including fabricated citations, undisclosed data sources, and images that look real but have no verifiable origin. The work here studies those failures and the rules, tools, and practices that researchers use to catch them. It treats governance as part of research method, not as paperwork added at the end.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are more settled than others. Authorship criteria and disclosure norms are widely discussed, but enforcement varies by journal, institution, and field. Fabricated citations are easy to generate and hard to detect at scale, so fact checking remains partly manual and partly automated. Training data provenance is often unknown, especially for large models, and researchers rarely have full visibility into what a model was trained on. Ethics review with AI assistance is emerging, but there is little agreement on what reviewers should ask or how to document AI use. Provenance for research images and data is improving through metadata, watermarking, and forensic analysis, yet determined manipulation can still evade routine checks, and no single tool or policy solves these problems.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a sequence from authorship to evidence. A reader asking who or what can be credited should begin with AI and Authorship, which covers contribution statements, ghostwriting, and the limits of current norms. Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking follows by showing how references are invented, how they are caught, and why verification still depends on the original paper rather than a search summary. Training Data and Academic Work looks upstream at the corpora and permissions behind models, including copyright, consent, and the difficulty of tracing data through a training pipeline. Ethics Review with AI Assistance addresses how boards and reviewers can evaluate projects that use AI, from risk assessment to documentation. Provenance of Research Images and Data closes the set by examining metadata, manipulation detection, and the chain of custody for figures and datasets, and the site's library holds 288 research papers that these pages treat as a working corpus for checking claims against original sources.
